concepts.name: Genesis and Background: Mountbatten Plan vs. Indian Independence Act
key_dimensions: Distinction between Mountbatten Plan (3 June Plan) as a political announcement and the Act as its legal instrument
Role of Attlee's announcement (February 1947) in setting the deadline for transfer of power
Why the original June 1948 deadline was advanced to August 1947 — political compulsions
UPSC trap: The Act was passed by British Parliament, NOT Indian Constituent Assembly

concepts.name: Partition of British India: Creation of Two Independent Dominions
key_dimensions: Section 1 of the Act: Creation of India and Pakistan as two separate independent dominions from 15 August 1947
Legal status of both dominions as equal successor states — neither was successor to British India
Distinction: Pakistan was a new creation; India continued international treaties and UN membership
UPSC trap: Pakistan did NOT automatically inherit India's UN seat; India did by continuity

concepts.name: Governor-General: Appointment, Powers, and Bifurcation
key_dimensions: Section 5: Each dominion to have its own Governor-General appointed by the King on the advice of the dominion cabinet
Mountbatten served as GG of India; Jinnah became GG of Pakistan (not Mountbatten) — UPSC favourite trap
Governor-General's power to adapt/modify laws for transitional governance under Section 9
Difference between GG's role under the Act vs. GG's role under GoI Act 1935 (residual powers)

concepts.name: Legislative Sovereignty of the Dominion Legislatures
key_dimensions: Section 6: Dominion legislatures granted full and unrestricted power to make laws — including laws repugnant to British laws
British Parliament could no longer legislate for the dominions without their consent
Significance: First time Indian legislature got true sovereign legislative power
Comparison with GoI Act 1935 where laws repugnant to British statutes were void

concepts.name: Constituent Assembly as Legislature: Dual Role
key_dimensions: Section 8: Constituent Assembly of each dominion to function as the dominion legislature until a new constitution was framed
Same body had two roles: constitution-making (Constituent Assembly) and law-making (Legislative Assembly)
UPSC trap: The Constituent Assembly of India passed ordinary legislation AND framed the Constitution simultaneously
Pakistan's Constituent Assembly also served this dual role until its constitution (1956)

concepts.name: Government of India Act 1935 as Interim Constitution
key_dimensions: Section 8: GoI Act 1935 to serve as the working constitution of both dominions until new constitutions were adopted
Modifications and adaptations made by GG under Section 9 to make it workable
Why GoI Act 1935 and NOT a new document — practical need for continuity and time constraints
Provisions of GoI Act 1935 that were dropped (e.g., Federal Court replaced by Supreme Court later)

concepts.name: Lapse of Paramountcy and the Princely States
key_dimensions: Section 7(b): All treaties and agreements with Indian States lapsed on 15 August 1947 — paramountcy ended
Princely states became technically 'independent' — they were NOT automatically merged into either dominion
UPSC trap: Paramountcy could NOT be transferred to dominion governments; it simply lapsed
Role of Sardar Patel and VP Menon in integrating states AFTER the Act — this was NOT mandated by the Act

concepts.name: Demise of the Crown's Suzerainty: Legal Implications
key_dimensions: Section 7(a): Crown's authority over British India ceased on 15 August 1947
Distinction between 'British India' (directly governed) and 'Indian States' (indirectly governed via paramountcy)
Both categories of Crown authority ended simultaneously through different legal mechanisms
UPSC trap: The King remained nominal head (as King of the dominions) until India became a republic in 1950

concepts.name: Demarcation of Boundaries: Radcliffe Award and the Act
key_dimensions: Act designated the boundaries of the two dominions with reference to the Radcliffe Commission's award
Section 3: Bengal and Punjab to be partitioned; boundary commissions headed by Sir Cyril Radcliffe
Interim arrangement: Until Radcliffe Award, existing provincial boundaries to apply (East and West Bengal/Punjab provisionally)
UPSC trap: Radcliffe Award was announced on 17 August 1947 — AFTER independence; boundaries were unknown on 15 August

concepts.name: Division of Armed Forces and Assets between the Two Dominions
key_dimensions: Act provided for division of Indian armed forces between India and Pakistan
Field Marshal Auchinleck appointed as Supreme Commander to oversee the partition of armed forces
Division of financial assets, liabilities, and the Reserve Bank of India's role as common banker initially
UPSC trap: Field Marshal Auchinleck's command was dissolved by 30 November 1947 — a temporary arrangement

concepts.name: Secretary of State for India: Abolition of the Office
key_dimensions: The office of Secretary of State for India was abolished by the Act
India Office in London also wound up — ending 90 years of direct British administrative oversight
Functions transferred to Commonwealth Relations Office
UPSC trap: Contrast with the India Act 1784 (Pitt's India Act) which created the Board of Control — the Act reversed this entire structure

concepts.name: Dominion Status: Nature, Implications, and Temporary Character
key_dimensions: Both India and Pakistan became dominions within the British Commonwealth — NOT fully independent republics immediately
Dominion status meant King George VI was the nominal head; GG acted on his behalf
India remained a dominion from 15 August 1947 to 26 January 1950; Pakistan until 23 March 1956
UPSC trap: India's membership of Commonwealth continued even after becoming a republic — 'London Declaration 1949' enabled this

concepts.name: Civil Services: Continuity, Protections, and Transitional Provisions
key_dimensions: Section 10: Existing civil servants retained their posts and service conditions until altered by the competent authority
Guarantee of service conditions — salaries, pensions could not be varied to their disadvantage without consent
ICS officers could opt for either dominion or take compensation for early retirement
UPSC trap: The Act guaranteed service conditions but did NOT permanently entrench them — legislatures could modify later

concepts.name: Sindh, Baluchistan, NWFP, and Sylhet: Special Provisions for Accession
key_dimensions: Referendum in NWFP (July 1947) to decide whether to join India or Pakistan — majority chose Pakistan
Sylhet referendum (July 1947): Muslim-majority Sylhet district of Assam voted to join Pakistan (East Bengal)
Baluchistan's Chief Commissioner's province and Sindh joined Pakistan without referendum
UPSC trap: The referendum in NWFP was NOT about independence — only about which dominion to join; Congress boycotted it

concepts.name: Bengal and Punjab: Partition Procedure and Constituent Assembly Representation
key_dimensions: Section 3: Legislative assemblies of Bengal and Punjab to meet in two parts to vote on partition
Western Punjab and Eastern Punjab, West Bengal and East Bengal became the divided entities
Members from divided provinces reallocated to respective dominion Constituent Assemblies
UPSC trap: The partition of Bengal in 1947 was the SECOND partition (first was 1905, reversed 1911) — different purposes and different outcomes

concepts.name: Position of Burma and Ceylon under the Act
key_dimensions: The Indian Independence Act 1947 did NOT cover Burma — Burma Independence Act was a separate legislation (1947)
Ceylon was granted independence separately under Ceylon Independence Act 1947
UPSC trap: All three acts were passed in 1947 but are distinct pieces of legislation with different structures
Burma chose to leave the Commonwealth entirely; Ceylon and India initially stayed as dominions

concepts.name: Adaptation of Laws: Governor-General's Transitional Powers under Section 9
key_dimensions: GG empowered to modify/adapt any existing Indian law to ensure smooth governance during transition
This power was meant to be temporary and transitional — not a permanent legislative override
Used extensively to adapt GoI Act 1935 — e.g., removal of Federal Court, modification of provincial structures
UPSC trap: This was an executive adaptation power, NOT a constituent power — GG could NOT use it to frame a new constitution

concepts.name: Termination of His Majesty's Appointment of Civil and Military Officers
key_dimensions: After 15 August 1947, the Crown no longer appointed Indian civil or military officers
Appointment power vested entirely in the dominion governments
Transition of command of armed forces from British to Indian/Pakistani governments
UPSC trap: British officers serving in Indian Army could continue on contract — their service was by agreement, not Crown appointment

concepts.name: Indian Independence Act 1947 vs. Government of India Act 1935: Comparative Constitutional Analysis
key_dimensions: GoI Act 1935: Federal structure with reserved powers, viceroy's overriding authority — Act 1947: Full dominion sovereignty
GoI Act 1935: Legislature's laws could be reserved for Crown's assent — Act 1947: No such reservation for dominion legislatures
GoI Act 1935: Governor-General had special responsibilities and discretionary functions — Act 1947: GG acts on cabinet advice
UPSC trap: The 1935 Act continued as working constitution under the 1947 Act, but its restrictive provisions were SUSPENDED not repealed

concepts.name: Historical Significance: End of the East India Company's Legal Legacy
key_dimensions: The Act symbolically ended the legal framework built since Regulating Act 1773 through successive legislation
Contrast: British entry via trade charter (1600) → exit via Parliamentary statute (1947) — full circle of legal transformation
The Act did NOT repeal GoI Act 1935 immediately — unlike previous acts which explicitly repealed predecessors
UPSC trap: East India Company was already abolished in 1858 (Government of India Act 1858) — the 1947 Act ended Crown's rule, not Company's
